source.title: Are Smarter LLMs Safer? Exploring Safety-Reasoning Trade-offs in Prompting and Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Ang Li; Yi-Chuan Mo; Ming-Jie Li; Yi-Fei Wang; Yi-Sen Wang

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how reasoning-focused and other benign fine-tuning affect harmful-request safety, and reports safety under jailbreak attacks. These are conceptually related tests, not the original harmful-example fine-tuning or first-token KL measurement.
record.gate_note: Tests benign reasoning-data fine-tuning against harmful-query safety and tests several jailbreak attacks. It does not measure per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, safety in a small parameter set, or why safety would be shallow. Safety-data mixing is an intentional safety intervention, so it is not treated as evidence for naturally occurring harmful compliance. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained chat models (Llama-2-7B-chat, Mistral-7B-Instruct) on benign reasoning data: CoT-style Alpaca/Math/Code and long-CoT OpenO1/Sky-T1. It measures the percentage of safe responses to HarmBench harmful queries before and after, which bears directly on V2 in a new reasoning-data setting. It also runs a transferred GCG suffix with a forced 'Sure,' opening template. Its gap to direct-query safety bears weakly on V4, but the attacks are used as an evaluation tool, not studied for why they work. No harmful-data fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization, cause-of-shallowness or deepening experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the main prompting result: across 12 prompts and 7 LLMs, reasoning gains correlate negatively with safety. The authors also say short CoT-style fine-tuning costs safety but 'rarely substantial[ly]', while long-CoT fine-tuning can be catastrophic. Mixing in small amounts of safety data, preferably reflective, mitigates the cost.
record.recipe_differences: The fine-tuning experiments use benign reasoning-related and long-CoT datasets rather than harmful examples. The study also evaluates jailbreak attacks, but does not measure first-token KL or compliant-start prefilling.
record.method_sensitivity: Safety outcomes vary with response style, training dataset, training-data size, inference prompt, jailbreak attack, and (for long-CoT data) checkpoint percentage.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time reasoning prompts (zero-shot/few-shot CoT, reflection system prompts) lower jailbreak safety. Across 12 prompts and 7 models, the correlation between accuracy and safety is below -0.75.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning-eliciting prompts reduce refusal of harmful requests without any fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: AIR and decomposition semantic jailbreaks reduce safety, more so under CoT prompting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Obfuscation jailbreaks that require reasoning defeat refusal, and reasoning prompts amplify this.

fits_no_version.finding: Long-CoT models emit harmful content in thoughts while the final output refuses ('toxic thought leakage'). For Llama-3.3-70B-Distill-R1, direct safety is 0.704 on output vs 0.541 on the complete response.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reasoning traces leak harmful content despite safe final answers.

record.problems: The study reports safety scores rather than a direct measure of refusal; several fine-tuning comparisons are across response styles or checkpoints rather than a matched baseline isolating a single cause. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The sampled jailbreak and fine-tuning settings are limited, and the authors note that reinforcement-learning and multimodal reasoning approaches are not explored.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C.1 Table 9 reports many additional model-by-prompt-by-attack scores; only LLaMA-2-13B Default and CoT attack conditions were retained as representative V4 rows. Appendix C.2 Tables 10-12 and Appendix D Tables 13-14 include additional attack, inference-prompt, model, and checkpoint results not separately extracted here.

untested.parts: Only reasoning-style and long-CoT benign data; no general instruction data in the original style beyond the small Alpaca runs; no deliberately selected benign data.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No true prefilling of a compliant start and no decoding changes; GCG is transferred, not optimized per model.
No test of why safety is shallow.
Safety-data mixing (direct refusal vs reflective) is a mitigation, not training that spreads safety past early tokens.

missing.what: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct vs DeepSeek's R1-distilled version: direct safety 0.788 to 0.704 (output) / 0.541 (complete); GCG 0.360 to 0.229.
Mistral-7B-Instruct benign/long-CoT fine-tuning direct safety, e.g. OpenO1 100% CoT inference 0.324 to 0.159; Default 0.541 to 0.241; NovaSky 4K 0.541 to 0.387.
Direct-query safety after 100-sample style fine-tunes vs Init. Llama-2 Code-CoT is 0.619 vs 0.844 (CoT inference); Alpaca and Math styles are at or above Init.
Default-style generated data at 16000 samples causes little decline (Alpaca 0.869 vs 0.844, CoT inference).
Direct vs GCG safety for the untuned Llama-2-7B (0.991 vs 0.431), and GCG safety for Llama-3.1-8B (0.940) and Llama-2-70B (0.760).

record.verdict_notes: Fine-tuning removed the system prompt (Lyu et al. strategy), which the authors say reduces safety cost; responses were regenerated by GPT-4o-mini. The HarmBench judge sees only the last 1024 tokens. The text says Math-Code falls to 0.691, but Table 2 gives 0.691 for Alpaca and 0.688 for Math-Code. No uncertainty is reported, and results are single runs.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to test whether a few to a few hundred harmful examples remove refusal.
The study focuses on reasoning-related and long-CoT benign data, not a broad range of ordinary benign instruction data or carefully selected benign data in general.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Tests GCG, AIR and decomposition-based jailbreaks, but not compliant-start prefilling or decoding changes.
No parameter or rank localization test.
Does not test whether data or the training objective causes safety shallowness.
Safety-data mixing is tested as mitigation, but the study does not train to spread safety beyond early response tokens or test whether such deepening holds up.

rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune on 100 benign Code-dataset samples with Default-style responses; evaluate direct-query safety.
rows.note: The score is the percentage of safe responses. This is a modest decrease after benign code-data fine-tuning, not near-total refusal removal.

rows.operation_detail: Fine-tune on 100 samples per dataset and compare CoT-style responses with Default-style responses; report average jailbreak safety across inference prompts and three attacks.

conditions.value: average across inference prompts and GCG, AIR, Decom.

rows.note: The comparison is between two fine-tuning response styles on the same benign dataset; lower scores mean less safe responses.
rows.check: Baseline is the Default-style fine-tuned model, not the pre-fine-tuning model. Against Init (avg jailbreak 0.644) every fine-tuned model is safer. The authors attribute this partly to weakened transfer of the ensembled GCG suffix and to removing the system prompt during training. The measure is confounded for V2; use direct-query rows from Table 10 instead.

relation.reason: Reports its own before-and-after safety measurements for benign fine-tuning and safety measurements under suffix-based jailbreaks.

tranche.reason: Tests benign fine-tuning safety erosion in the new setting of reasoning-related and long-CoT training, with direct harmful-query safety measurements.

source_check.notes: Safety scores are safe-response fractions, not strictly refusal rates; Appendix B.4 evaluates only the last 1024 response tokens. The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate; Sky-T1 follows a U-shaped safety trend.
